parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which single component only lets current through in one direction, so it can cut off one half of the a.c. input.
parts.proper_answer: Insert a diode in series in the top lead, with forward direction from $V_{IN}$ toward $V_{OUT}$ (triangle points to the right, bar on the right).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what half-wave means**
You need current to reach the output on one half-cycle but to be blocked on the opposite half-cycle. That one-way behaviour is exactly what a diode gives you.

Step 2: **Place and orient the diode**
Put the diode in the gap in the top wire in series. For the positive $V_{IN}$ shown in Fig. 5.2 to appear at the output, the anode is on the left ($V_{IN}$ side) and the cathode is on the right ($V_{OUT}$ side). The symbol is a triangle pointing right with a vertical bar at its tip: $$ \text{anode } \triangleright| \text{ cathode} $$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
key_concepts: charge storage and discharge through load
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the capacitor does when the diode stops conducting - where does the resistor get its current from?
parts.proper_answer: $V_{OUT}$ is smoothed - ripple is reduced so $V_{OUT}$ falls only slowly when the diode is off.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture charging and discharging**
When the diode conducts, the capacitor charges quickly up to the peak voltage. When the diode blocks, the capacitor cannot discharge back through the diode, so it discharges slowly through the $14\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor.

Step 2: **Link to the output shape**
That stored charge keeps current flowing in the resistor, so $V_{OUT}$ stays high instead of dropping to zero. In other words the capacitor smooths $V_{OUT}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 5.2 and find the time for one complete repeat of the square wave, for example from one rising edge to the next rising edge.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the period from Fig. 5.2**
The pattern $+5.5\text{ V}$ then $-5.5\text{ V}$ repeats. One rising edge is at $t = 0$, the next rising edge is at $t = 0.040\text{ s}$. So $$ T = 0.040\text{ s} $$

Step 2: **Convert period to frequency**
Frequency and period are reciprocals: $$ f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{0.040} = 25\text{ Hz} $$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Identify on Fig. 5.3 where the smooth discharge starts and ends, and read the starting voltage $V_0$ and the voltage after that discharge time.
Hint 2: Recall how the discharge equation links $V$, $V_0$, discharge time $t$ and $\tau$, then rearrange with logarithms to solve for $\tau$.
parts.proper_answer: Discharge from $V_0 = 5.50\text{ V}$ for $t = 0.020\text{ s}$ to $V = 3.25\text{ V}$. Using $V = V_0 \exp(-t/\tau)$ gives $3.25 = 5.50 \exp(-0.020/\tau)$, so $\tau = 0.038\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick the discharge section**
In Fig. 5.3 the flat top at about $5.50\text{ V}$ ends at $t = 0.020\text{ s}$ when $V_{IN}$ goes negative. The output then decays until $t = 0.040\text{ s}$. So discharge time is $$ t = 0.040 - 0.020 = 0.020\text{ s} $$ with $V_0 = 5.50\text{ V}$ and final $V \approx 3.25\text{ V}$.

Step 2: **Apply the exponential decay law**
For discharge through a resistor: $$ V = V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{RC}\right) = V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau}\right) $$ where $\tau = RC$. Substitute the readings: $$ 3.25 = 5.50 \exp\left(-\frac{0.020}{\tau}\right) $$

Step 3: **Solve for $\tau$**
Rearrange: $$ \frac{3.25}{5.50} = \exp\left(-\frac{0.020}{\tau}\right) $$ Take natural log: $$ \ln\left(\frac{3.25}{5.50}\right) = -\frac{0.020}{\tau} $$ This gives $\tau \approx 0.038\text{ s}$, as required.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which two components set how slowly the capacitor discharges, and how their values combine into the time constant.
Hint 2: Check the resistor value is in ohms before rearranging for $C$, and remember to give a capacitance unit.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the time constant relation**
The discharge rate is set by both $R$ and $C$: $$ \tau = RC $$ So you can get $C$ from $\tau$ and $R$.

Step 2: **Substitute with correct units**
$\tau = 0.038\text{ s}$ and $R = 14\text{ k}\Omega = 14000\text{ }\Omega$. Then: $$ C = \frac{\tau}{R} = \frac{0.038}{14000} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F} $$ That is about $2.7\text{ }\mu\text{F}$.

parts.label: (c)
key_concepts: continuous charging and constant smoothed output
hints: Hint 1: Compare the positive and negative parts of $V_{IN}$ in Fig. 5.2 - what is the same about their size?
Hint 2: Think about what a full-wave rectifier does to a negative input, and whether the capacitor ever gets time to discharge if it is topped up on every half-cycle.
parts.proper_answer: $V_{IN}$ has the same constant magnitude of about $5.5\text{ V}$ in both positive and negative half-cycles, so after full-wave rectification the input to the capacitor is always $+5.5\text{ V}$. Hence $V_{OUT}$ is now constant at about $5.5\text{ V}$ and does not decay.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See what full-wave does to this special input**
Fig. 5.2 is a square wave switching between $+5.5\text{ V}$ and $-5.5\text{ V}$. Full-wave rectification flips the negative half to positive, so the rectified voltage is $+5.5\text{ V}$ all the time.

Step 2: **Explain the steady output**
Because the capacitor is always connected through conducting diodes to $+5.5\text{ V}$, it stays fully charged and has no interval in which it must discharge through the resistor alone. So $V_{OUT}$ remains constant at the peak value instead of showing the saw-tooth decay of Fig. 5.3.
